The Art of Being Between

There is a particular feeling that arrives at about 2:47 in the afternoon on a day with no urgent obligations. The sun is at an angle that makes dust visible in the air. The refrigerator hums. You are not sad, not happy, not bored in the sharp way that makes you reach for your phone. You are just... there. Suspended. It’s a feeling we don’t have a good word for in English, which is strange because it might be the most common human feeling of all: the quiet astonishment of simply existing without needing to do anything about it.

I think about that feeling a lot.

If you had told me as a child that adulthood would be mostly made of these in-between moments — waiting for water to boil, standing in line at the post office, watching a washing machine finish its cycle — I would have been disappointed. Childhood is so narrative. Everything feels like it’s leading somewhere: you will grow up, you will learn to drive, you will understand algebra, you will fall in love, you will become an astronaut or a veterinarian. Life is a series of locked doors and you are collecting keys.

No one tells you that eventually you stop collecting keys and just start appreciating the hallway.

And the hallway is, it turns out, extraordinary.

### 1. The Scale of Things

Let's start big, because we are so rarely allowed to.

You are standing on a sphere of molten rock wrapped in a thin, cool skin, spinning at roughly a thousand miles per hour, orbiting a medium-sized star that is itself racing around the center of a galaxy that contains between two hundred and four hundred billion other stars. That galaxy is one of about two trillion galaxies we can observe, and we can only observe about five percent of what the universe is actually made of. The rest is dark matter and dark energy, which we have named with the scientific equivalent of a shrug: "dark," meaning "we don't know what this is, but it has to be there or the math doesn't work."

All of this has been expanding for 13.8 billion years from a point smaller than an atom.

Now, let's go small.

Inside your body right now, about thirty-seven trillion cells are doing their jobs. Each one contains DNA that, if unwound, would be about six feet long. If you unwound all the DNA in your body end to end, it would stretch from the Earth to the Sun and back over six hundred times. Your blood is not red when it’s inside you — it only looks red when it hits the oxygen outside. You have more bacterial cells in you than human cells. You are a walking ecosystem, a collaborative project.

And then there is the middle scale, the human scale: the scale of mugs and door handles and the particular way your friend laughs when they are trying not to laugh. We live in the middle, but we are made of extremes.

What I find most moving about this is not that we are tiny or that we are huge, but that we can comprehend both at all. A brain made of fat and salt water, evolved to keep a bipedal ape alive on the savanna long enough to reproduce, can also understand general relativity and write symphonies and ache for a person who lives on another continent. We are the universe's way of looking at itself, which sounds like a line from a greeting card until you really let it sink in and realize that Carl Sagan wasn't being poetic, he was being literal.

You are literally stardust that has become self-aware. The carbon in your left hand was forged in a different star than the carbon in your right hand. You should, from time to time, sit with that.

### 2. In Praise of Boredom

We have declared war on boredom, and we are winning, and that is a tragedy.

A hundred years ago, boredom was inevitable. You stared out the window on a train. You waited for bread to rise. You sat on a porch while the evening came. Your mind, with nowhere to go, would start to wander. It would make odd connections. It would remember the argument you had three years ago and rewrite it. It would invent a story. It would notice how the light hit the leaves.

Now we have a small rectangle of infinite novelty in our pockets, and the moment boredom approaches, we banish it. We scroll. We refresh. We optimize our spare seconds.

But boredom is not a bug. It's a feature. It's the compost from which creativity grows.

Neuroscientists have found that when you are "doing nothing," your brain is not doing nothing at all. It activates what is called the Default Mode Network — a constellation of regions that lights up when you are daydreaming, remembering, imagining the future, and thinking about what other people are thinking. It's the network that allows for self-reflection, for moral reasoning, for constructing a sense of identity over time. It's the part of you that does its best work when you are looking out a window and not trying to be productive.

Every great idea I have ever had, and every paragraph I’ve ever written that I actually liked, arrived while I was doing something else: washing dishes, walking without headphones, sitting on a bus and deliberately not looking at my phone. They came from boredom. They came from making space.

We talk a lot about mindfulness now, and mindfulness is wonderful. But I want to make a case for mindlessness — for the gentle, aimless, unoptimized wandering of a mind that is left alone for ten minutes. Next time you are waiting for something — the microwave, the elevator, a friend who is running late — try not to fill it. Let the boredom arrive. See what it brings with it. It might bring nothing, and that is also valuable. Learning to be comfortable with nothing is a superpower in a world that is constantly trying to sell you something.

### 3. The Secret Lives of Objects

If you look around whatever room you are in right now, you are surrounded by ghosts.

That chair you are sitting on — someone designed it, someone else manufactured it, someone drove the truck that delivered it, someone wrote the invoice for it. The wood in it grew for decades somewhere, drinking rain and sunlight. The metal screws were mined from somewhere deep in the Earth.

The t-shirt you are wearing has probably traveled more miles than you have. The cotton was grown in one country, spun into yarn in another, sewn together in a third, and shipped to you in a container that crossed an ocean. How many hands touched it before it touched you?

Even the most mundane object has a story that would fill a novel if we bothered to listen. And we almost never do, because we have been trained to see objects as disposable. Use, discard, upgrade. But objects are patient. They hold memory.

I have a chipped blue mug that I have used for tea every morning for eight years. It is not a beautiful mug. It was free, from a conference I barely remember. But the chip on the rim fits exactly where my lower lip goes. The inside is stained a faint brown that no amount of scrubbing removes. If it broke tomorrow, I would be disproportionately sad, not because I couldn't replace it, but because I couldn't replace *it*. The eight years of mornings are in it.

We live in an economy that wants us to believe that new is always better. But there is a kind of wisdom in old things. A pair of shoes broken in to the shape of your feet. A book with notes in the margins from a younger version of yourself. A kitchen table with rings from a thousand meals.

There is a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi*, which finds beauty in imperfection, impermanence, and incompleteness. There is a related practice called *kintsugi*, where broken pottery is repaired with gold, making the cracks part of its history rather than something to hide. I think we need to apply kintsugi to more than just pottery.

Your life will crack. That is not a failure; that is how the light gets in, and also how your particular history becomes visible.

### 4. Language is Time Travel

Consider this: right now, you are hearing a voice in your head that is not your own. It is my voice, or rather, a voice you are inventing to represent me, as you read these words. These words were written at a different time than when you are reading them. I may be asleep. I may be dead. And yet, here we are, thinking together.

Language is the closest thing we have to telepathy. And also to time travel.

When you read a letter written by a soldier two hundred years ago, or a grocery list left on a counter by someone you love who just stepped out, you are collapsing time. A person who lived before electricity, who never saw an airplane, can still make you laugh with a joke they wrote in ink by candlelight. Sappho wrote fragments of poems on papyrus over two thousand years ago, and we can still feel the exact texture of her heartbreak.

And it’s not just the grand literature. Everyday language is a museum.

The word "clue" originally meant a ball of yarn, from the Greek myth where Theseus used a ball of yarn — a *clew* — to find his way out of the labyrinth after killing the Minotaur. So when you say you are "looking for a clue," you are metaphorically holding a ball of yarn in a maze.

The word "disaster" means "bad star" — from the Latin *dis* (bad) and *aster* (star). The ancients blamed catastrophes on unfavorable astrological alignments.

Every word is a fossil. Every sentence is an archaeology.

What’s even stranger is that language is not just describing reality, it is creating it. The words we have available shape what we can think. There is a famous, though debated, example of the Sámi people having hundreds of words for snow and reindeer, because those distinctions matter for survival. Whether or not that number is exact, the principle is true: we notice what we have words for.

So inventing new language, or learning someone else's language, is literally learning to see new colors.

This is why I love dictionaries, and etymology, and untranslatable words. Like *toska* in Russian — a spiritual ache, a yearning with no object. Like *mamihlapinatapai* in Yaghan — a wordless, meaningful look shared by two people who both want to start something but neither wants to go first. Like *ubuntu* in Nguni Bantu — "I am because we are."

We need these words. Let’s collect them like keys, but this time to open doors inward.

### 5. Entropy, Love, and Laundry

The second law of thermodynamics states, in simple terms, that everything tends toward disorder. Entropy always increases. Your room gets messy on its own; it never gets tidy on its own. Stars burn out. Ice melts. Mountains erode.

It is the most depressing law of physics and also the most romantic.

Because life, for a brief moment, does the opposite. Life is a local, temporary rebellion against entropy. You eat food, you grow, you heal a cut, you keep your house from falling down, you sort your books alphabetically. You create order at the cost of enormous energy.

And love — love is the most entropy-defying thing we do.

Love is saying: I will choose this one person, this one family, this one friendship, and I will give it my attention, my time, my maintenance. I will remember your birthday. I will listen to the same story you tell for the fifth time. I will do the dishes even though I know they will get dirty again tomorrow. I will stay.

All relationships are a practice of fighting entropy together. They decay if left alone. They require input. That is not a flaw in love; that *is* love. The work is the love.

That is why laundry is secretly profound. Laundry is Sisyphean. You wash the clothes, you wear them, they get dirty, you wash them again, forever until you die. It is objectively pointless if you view it as a task to be completed. But if you view it as a ritual of care — I am keeping my family warm, I am keeping my body respected, I am participating in the endless, beautiful maintenance of being alive — then it becomes something else entirely.

The same is true for making a bed, for sweeping a floor, for sending a text that says "thinking of you." None of these things will last. That is precisely why they matter.

We want monuments. We want our lives to be permanent and significant. But perhaps significance is not in permanence at all. Perhaps it is in the willingness to do the temporary things over and over with love. A Tibetan monk spends weeks creating an intricate sand mandala grain by grain, only to sweep it away upon completion. The point was never the mandala. The point was the making.

Your life is a sand mandala that you are making and sweeping away simultaneously. Make it colorful anyway.

### 6. An Invitation Back to the Hallway

So here we are, back in the hallway, in that 2:47 pm light.

I don't know what you are carrying today as you read this. Maybe you are full of purpose and momentum. Maybe you are anxious and scrolling to avoid a feeling. Maybe you are grieving something no one else can see. Whatever it is, you are allowed to put it down for five minutes.

Look up from this screen. Really look at where you are.

Notice three things you have never noticed before in this room. The way the paint meets the ceiling. A shadow. The sound your building makes. The temperature of the air on your skin.

Take one slow breath, not because it will optimize you or make you more productive, but just because breathing is a quietly miraculous thing that you have done about twenty thousand times today without thanking yourself once.

Remember that you are not behind. The timeline is invented. A tree does not feel behind because it hasn't grown fruit yet. A star does not hurry.

And if you can, do one small, entropy-defying act of care in the next hour. Not a grand gesture. Water a plant. Text someone something kind and true that you have been meaning to say. Wash that mug. Let a little order bloom from your hands.

You don't need to write freely for 2500 words to make something meaningful. You just need to live freely for five minutes.

But since you asked me to write freely — thank you for giving me this hallway. Thank you for walking down it with me for a little while. It’s been lovely to think out loud in your company.

Wherever you go next, I hope you notice the dust in the light.
